DOCUMENT:
"""
Purpose: To develop and evaluate a locally deployed multi-agent AI system for radiology report structuring and quality assurance.

Introduction: Structured radiology reporting is essential for clear communication and quality assurance, yet variability in report formats and content can hinder consistency and patient care. Automated tools that standardize report structure and flag quality issues may improve reporting practices. This study aims to address these challenges by developing and evaluating a multi-agent AI system for structuring and quality assurance of radiology reports.

Materials and Methods:

Dataset: This retrospective study included 638 radiology reports from CT examinations of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis dictated by 15 board-certified radiologists in 2023 and 2024 at a single institution. Reports were selected consecutively from routine clinical practice without exclusion criteria. The use of reports from only 15 radiologists may introduce bias related to individual reporting styles and institutional practices, potentially limiting the diversity of language and structure encountered by the AI system and affecting the generalizability of the results.

AI System Development: A locally deployed multi-agent AI system was developed, consisting of specialized agents with distinct roles. The structuring agent segmented reports into standardized anatomical sections at the sentence level. This was achieved using pattern-matching rules (regular expressions) to identify anatomical terms and section headers, combined with locally run large language models (LLMs). The LLMs were based on open-source transformer architectures (e.g., Llama 2), fine-tuned on a corpus of de-identified radiology reports from the institution, and deployed on secure local servers to ensure data privacy and compliance. The system included several QA agents: (1) a section mismatch agent that detected inconsistencies between the Findings and Impression sections, (2) an intra-section consistency agent that identified contradictions within sections, (3) a gender-anatomy conflict agent that flagged gender-specific anatomical inconsistencies, and (4) a critical findings agent that checked for documentation of communication regarding critical findings. Agents operated in sequence, with the output of the structuring agent serving as input for the QA agents, and each agent’s output was passed to the next for further analysis.

Evaluation Process: The evaluation phase was conducted separately from system development. Two board-certified radiologists independently evaluated a subset of 45 reports that had been restructured and flagged by the system. Each radiologist reviewed the reports using the following criteria: (1) accuracy of anatomical structuring (correct assignment of sentences to anatomical sections), (2) retention of original clinical content (no loss of clinically relevant information), (3) absence of fabricated information (no addition of content not present in the original report), and (4) overall QA performance. Radiologists applied these criteria by directly comparing the original and restructured reports side-by-side, noting any discrepancies in section assignment, missing or added information, and the appropriateness of QA flags. QA performance was rated as "excellent" (no errors and all issues correctly flagged), "good" (minor errors or missed flags not affecting clinical interpretation), or "fair" (significant errors or missed issues that could impact clinical care). Disagreements were resolved by discussion, and the nature of disagreements was recorded to identify potential system limitations. Inter-rater agreement was measured using Cohen’s kappa statistic, which quantifies the level of agreement between two raters beyond chance (values between 0.61–0.80 indicate substantial agreement).

Results:

The multi-agent AI system structured the Findings sections of all 638 reports (22,270 sentences) into a predefined anatomical format while retaining the original report content. The system flagged 90 reports (14.1% of 638), most commonly for section mismatches (80 reports, 12.5%). In the radiologist evaluation of 45 reports, both reviewers agreed that 31 (69%) were correctly restructured, 2 (4%) were incorrectly restructured, and disagreed on 12 (27%), yielding a Cohen’s kappa of 0.62, indicating substantial agreement between reviewers. Cohen’s kappa was calculated by comparing the number of agreements and disagreements in categorical ratings of report structuring, adjusted for the agreement expected by chance. Disagreements primarily involved borderline cases of anatomical section assignment (e.g., sentences describing findings at anatomical boundaries such as the diaphragm) and interpretation of ambiguous sentences (e.g., statements like "no acute abnormality" without clear anatomical reference). These cases were resolved through consensus discussion, with reviewers considering clinical context and standard reporting conventions. Both reviewers agreed that no clinically important information was omitted and no fabricated content was introduced. Overall QA performance was rated as "excellent" in 28 reports (62%), "good" in 10 reports (22%), and "fair" in 7 reports (16%).

Conclusion:

A locally deployed multi-agent AI system combined radiology report structuring and quality assurance within a single workflow, demonstrating favorable performance in radiologist evaluation. The retrospective design and use of a single-institution dataset may limit generalizability, as results could be influenced by local reporting practices and the small number of radiologists. These limitations may result in the system being less effective when applied to reports with different styles, terminologies, or institutional conventions. To address these limitations, future work should include a prospective validation phase in which the system is integrated into clinical workflows and its performance is monitored in real time. Additionally, expanding the dataset to include reports from multiple institutions and a larger, more diverse group of radiologists will help increase linguistic and structural diversity, reducing bias and improving generalizability. For ambiguous language, future iterations of the system should incorporate advanced natural language processing techniques, such as context-aware language models and consensus-based rules for anatomical section assignment, as well as active learning approaches where ambiguous cases are flagged for human review and used to iteratively refine the model. Such systems may support standardization of reporting and quality assurance in radiology practice.
